lines.text: אכר 47 אכל
scarcely. Gen. 27, 30 אַךְ יָצֹא יָצָא יַעֲקֹב
וְעֵשָׂו אָחִיו בָּא—and Jacob was scarce
gone out.... when Esau his brother came
in. Judg. 7, 19.—So Lat. tantum quod,
Cic. ad Fam. 8. 23, “tantum quod ex
Arpinati veneram, cum mihi a te litteræ
redditæ sint.” Vellei. 2. 117.
* אָכַד obsol. root, i. q. עָקַד, אָגַד, to
bind; then to strengthen, to fortify a
city. Hence
אַכַּד (fortress, castle) Accad, pr. n. of
a city built by Nimrod, Gen. 10, 10. Sept.
Ἀρχάδ, comp. דַּמֶּשֶׂק and דַּרְמֶשֶׂק. The
Targums and Jerome understand Nesi-
bis a city of Mesopotamia.
אַכְזָב (for כָּזָב, Aleph. prosthet. r. כָּזַב)
pr. falsehood, deceit, but every where
concr. for נַחַל אַכְזָב a deceitful brook, a
failing torrent, soon drying up and dis-
appointing the hope of the traveller,
Jer. 15, 18. Mic. 1, 14. Opp. אֵיתָן a per-
ennial stream. Comp. Lat. fundus men-
dax Hor. Carm. 3. 1. 30.
אַכְזִיב (i. q. אַכְזָב) Achzib, pr. n. a)
A city on the sea-coast of Asher, be-
tween Acco and Tyre, Gr. Ecdippa, now
called ez-Zîb. Josh. 19, 29. Judg. 1, 31.
b) A city in the tribe of Judah, Josh.
15, 44. Mic. 1, 14. Comp. כְּזִיב and כֹּזְבָה.
אַכְזָר m. (r. כָּזַר) pr. violence, but every
where as concr. violent, Lam. 4, 3. Job
30, 21. Of poison, violent, deadly, Deut.
32, 33.—Once in a good sense for bold,
brave, Job 41, 2.—Hence
אַכְזָרִי fierce, cruel, Prov. 5, 9. Jer. 6,
23. Also cruel, terrible; Prov. 17, 11 a
terrible messenger, who brings fatal tid-
ings, as of a sentence of death. Is. 13, 9.
אַכְזְרִיּוּת f. (from אַכְזָרִי with the end-
ing וּת, see Heb. Gram. § 85. 6,) fierce-
ness, cruelty. of wrath Prov. 27, 4.
אֲכִילָה f. an eating, a meal, 1 K. 19, 8.
R. אָכַל.
אָכִישׁ (r. אָבַשׁ) Achish, pr. n. of a king
of the Philistines in Gath, 1 Sam. 21, 11.
* אָכַל inf. constr. אֱכֹל, with pref. לֶאֱכֹל,
בֶּאֱכֹל, c. suff. אֲכָלְךָ, אָכְלוֹ; fut. יֹאכַל, in
pause יֹאכֵל, once יוֹכְלוּ Ez. 42, 5.
1. to eat, to eat up, to devour; absol.
Deut. 27, 7. 1 Sam. 9, 13; oftener with
acc. of food; rarely לְ Lam. 4, 5; בְּ Ex.
25, 22. Num. 15, 19, comp. ἐσθίειν τινός.
Spoken not only very frequently of
men, but also of beasts, Is. 11, 7; whence
הָאֹכֵל the eater, in Samson’s riddle
Judg. 14, 14, is the lion, comp. Arab.
الآكِلُ.—The following phrases are to be
noted: a) to eat of a land, a field, a vine,
i. e. to eat the fruit of them, Gen. 3, 17.
vour sacrifices; spoken of idols in allusion
to the lectisternia, Deut. 32, 38. Ez.16,20.
c) אָכַל לֶחֶם to eat bread, i. q. to take food,
1 K. 21, 7. Ps. 102, 5; with לֹא, not to
take food, to fast, 1 Sam. 28, 20. 30, 12.
Also, to take a meal, to dine or sup. to
comp. φαγεῖν ἄρτον Luke 14, 1. Some-
times אָכַל לֶחֶם is simply i. q. to live, Am.
7, 12. d) אָכַל לִפְנֵי יְהוָֹה to eat before
Jehovah, spoken of the sacrificial feasts
held in the temple, Deut. 12, 7. 18. 14, 23.
Ex. 18, 12. e) to eat the flesh of any one,
Ps. 27, 2, spoken of fierce and cruel ene-
mies, thirsting for one’s blood.—Differ-
ent is f) to eat one’s own flesh, Eccl. 4, 5,
spoken of the fool devoured by envy.
Comp. Hom. Il. 6. 202 ὃν θυμὸν κατέδων.
g) עֲנִיִּים, אֲכַל הָעָם, to eat up or devour a
people, the poor, spoken of rulers or no-
bles who consume the wealth of a peo-
ple by oppression and extortion, Ps. 14, 4.
Prov. 30, 14. Hab. 3, 15. Comp. δημοβό-
ρος βασιλεύς Il. 1. 231. So also to devour
the flesh of a people id. Mic. 3, 3. Else-
where to eat, to devour, is i. q. to consume
in war, by slaughter, Hos. 7, 7. Is. 9, 11.
51, 34. Comp. Judith 5, 24. h) to eat
or devour the words of any one, i. e. to
receive them greedily, to listen eagerly;
Gr. φαγεῖν ῥήματα, dicta devorare, Plaut.
Asin. 3. 3. 59. So Jer. 15, 16 נִמְצְאוּ
דְבָרֶיךָ וָאֹכְלֵם thy words were brought to
me, and I did eat them, i. e. devoured
them eagerly, made them wholly mine.
(Comp. ad Carm. Samarit. 4. 16.) Hence
is to be explained the vision of the roll
or volume given to the prophet to be
devoured, Ez. 2, 8. 3, 1 sq. comp. Rev.
2. to devour, to consume, often spoken

line_status.note: Headword middle letter is a rounded כ (not ב with a right-projecting foot) and ends in plain ד, not final ךְ; the second comparandum's middle letter has a descender below the baseline, so it is ק (עָקַד), not ב. Matches Gesenius's entry for the root of אַכָּד "to bind".
The mark after "Ecdippa" is a single comma sitting on the baseline (the italic a's tail runs into it); there is no upper dot forming a semicolon, so Reading B is correct.
Under the zayin of the last word the print shows two vertically stacked dots (shewa), not a horizontal tsere; so כֹּזְבָה, matching Reading B.
The punctuation after "Gath" has a visible tail descending below the baseline, so it is a comma (Reading B), not a period (Reading A).

First suffixed form: the aleph carries a hateph-pathah (two vertical dots plus stroke) and the kaph a qamets, i.e. אֲכָלְךָ (Reading A); the following form אָכְלוֹ has qamets under aleph and shva under kaph, which is what Reading B wrongly copied onto the first word.

The only disagreement is the dash in 43-45: the printed stroke is short (narrower than a digit), a hyphen, not an en dash. Everything else (מִן with hireq, no yod; punctuation) agrees with both readings.
A damma is printed above the final lām (a small hook above the tall lām stroke at the far left), so the word ends ـلُ; Reading A omits it.
After "sacrifices" the mark has a dot above the comma tail — a semicolon, not a plain comma, so Reading B is correct.

The two readings differ only in spacing within the final reference. The print is set tight at line end: "Ez.16,20." has no visible space after "Ez." or after the comma, whereas "Deut. 32, 38." does have spaces. Reading A reproduces the printed spacing; B normalises it.

The decisive difference is item order: printed left-to-right the first Hebrew item after "g)" is עֲנִיִּים (with dagesh in the yod), followed by a comma, then אֲכַל הָעָם, comma — Reading B's order. Reading A swaps the two items. Vowel points otherwise match both readings.
